title: What consistent really means
summary: Choose the guarantee for each operation and name what a partition changes.

steps.title: The balance and the activity list disagree
steps.text: A transfer succeeds. The balance screen shows the debit, but a refreshed activity list does not. Later, a refresh shows an even older list. These are different failures. A product can need a current balance, read-your-writes on confirmation, and monotonic reads while paging history without demanding the same guarantee everywhere.

steps.title: Separate time from transactions
steps.text: Linearizability makes each operation appear to take effect at one instant between its call and reply, respecting real-time order. Serializability makes concurrent transactions equivalent to some serial order. That order need not respect wall-clock order; strict serializability adds that requirement. Snapshot isolation lets a transaction read a stable committed snapshot and usually prevents conflicting writes to the same item. It can still allow write skew across different items. Read-your-writes prevents your later reads missing your own successful writes. Monotonic reads prevent a session moving backwards through versions. Neither session guarantee alone makes every reader see the latest value.

steps.title: Worked example: nobody is on call
steps.text: Two doctors are on call. Each transaction reads a snapshot with both doctors present, checks that another doctor remains, and turns its own row off. They write different rows, so snapshot isolation can let both commit. The result has zero doctors. Serializable execution would reject at least one transaction or force it to see the first change. Locking a shared roster guard or encoding the invariant in one atomic record can also work. This is a transaction schedule, not a demo: the sim cannot execute concurrent SQL transactions.

rows.label: Write skew outcome
rows.how: Two snapshots see 2; each removes a different doctor

rows.label: Remote coordination floor
rows.how: 10 ms local path + 80 ms required RTT

rows.label: Session catch-up
rows.how: 300 writes/s × 2 s lag; a version token can require waiting

steps.q: A balance transaction is serializable. Does that word alone promise every later reader the latest balance?
choices: No, real-time ordering and read routing need their own guarantees
Only if the rows have timestamps
steps.why: Transaction isolation and the freshness of a later read are different properties.

steps.q: Why is saying our database is strongly consistent insufficient? Follow-up: choose guarantees for three screens.
checklist: Name linearizability, transaction isolation and session behavior separately
Tie each guarantee to a user-visible harm
steps.model: I need to know which operations, which replicas and which failure conditions that phrase covers. A last-seat reservation needs an atomic invariant, often a serializable transaction or conditional write. A save confirmation needs read-your-writes, perhaps by routing to an authority or waiting for a version. A public count can accept bounded staleness. During a partition I would defer the reservation, keep a local pending edit visible and label stale public data. The latency and availability costs differ by screen.

steps.title: Partitions and ordinary days
steps.text: CAP says that during a network partition you cannot guarantee both linearizable behavior and a successful response to every request at every nonfailed node. Its availability definition is stricter than an uptime percentage. It does not say pick two features forever, and partition tolerance is not a convenient switch in a real network. Outside partitions, PACELC asks what latency you pay for coordination to get the chosen consistency. Suppose an app and local store take 10 ms while a remote round trip takes 80 ms. A protocol requiring that remote reply has a rough floor near 90 ms. Choose per screen: session versions or primary reads for confirmation, a serializable reservation for the last seat, and bounded staleness for a public count. State how each screen behaves while separated.

steps.q: Both doctors leave under snapshot isolation. Which remedy addresses the actual invariant?
choices: Serialize through a shared guard or use serializable transactions with retries
steps.why: The invariant spans two rows. Checking separate snapshots and writing separate rows does not protect it.

steps.q: Why not make every read linearizable? Follow-up: we have users an ocean away.
checklist: Consider local and cached reads with narrower guarantees
Keep a strong authority where harm warrants it
steps.model: A remote authority may add roughly an ocean round trip to each request. Some protocols can serve safe local reads, but only under explicit lease, quorum or leadership rules. I would spend that coordination on decisions such as allocating money or stock, and avoid it for public summaries. The test is whether a stale result can cause harm and what the next action validates. A faster stale summary still needs a clear freshness promise.

steps.q: A partition isolates a region from the primary. What is a defensible product policy?
choices: Serve a marked stale public count but defer exclusive seat claims
Promise every operation is latest and available there
Call the entire product AP and stop specifying screens
steps.why: Guarantees belong to operations. Stale public data may be acceptable where conflicting reservations are not.

takeaway: Ask which operation, which order and which failure, then choose the smallest sufficient guarantee.
